The deadline's Nov. 22. Williams Lake residents have until Sunday, Nov. 22 to drop off gift-filled shoeboxes at Evangelical Free Church for this year’s Operation Christmas Child drive. Kathy Shetler, a Williams Lake volunteer with Operation Christmas Child, has been involved since the mid 1990s when she began packing shoeboxes at Maranatha Christian School in Williams Lake. She has since helped lead the project locally, coordinate drop-offs and work with churches. Shetler said Williams Lake shipped 451 shoeboxes in 2025, with about 50 more donated online. She hopes to match or exceed last year’s in-person total. Operation Christmas Child is a Samaritan’s Purse project that works with local churches and ministries overseas to distribute gift-filled shoeboxes to children at Christian outreach events. Shetler suggested packing school supplies, hygiene items, a toy or craft kit and something to wear, such as a hat or gloves. Donors can choose to pack for a child ages two to four, five to nine or 10 to 14. Shetler asked donors to leave out candy, liquids, toothpaste, soap, glass items and war-themed toys. Shetler thanked Williams Lake residents for their generosity over the years. “It’s such an expression of love and compassion to children around the world that do not have much,” she said. Empty shoeboxes and brochures are available at the Evangelical Free Church, 1100 North 11th Ave., and at Kit and Kaboodle, 83A Second Ave. S. Filled shoeboxes can be dropped off at the church through Sunday, Nov. 22. Shetler said the boxes will travel through Kamloops to Calgary, where they’ll be checked before being shipped overseas.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session as the new Conservative government gets its bearings in the short window between being sworn in and the holiday season. “Our government has an ambitious agenda, and we want to ensure legislation is properly prepared and receives the debate and consideration it deserves,” Doerkson said in a written statement on Monday (Nov. 16). The B.C. Conservative Party will have a large majority in the legislature when it does convene, after the party won 64 of 93 seats in the Oct. 24 election. Doerkson had left the door open to recalling the legislature for a short session before the end of the year as he seeks to pursue a slate of changes after nine years of NDP government. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Thursday evening. The premier and cabinet will then be sworn in on Friday, officially taking the reins of the B.C. government. “Ministers will get to work from day one, advancing our priorities and preparing a substantive legislative agenda for the spring,” Doerkson said. The incoming government can accomplish a lot simply by taking administrative control of the various government ministries and by issuing cabinet orders. This could include changes to the Massey Tunnel project. Doerkson has promised to scrap the tunnel and build a bridge instead. The new government could also get started building other infrastructure, like the promised urgent care centres and Surrey women’s and children’s hospital. Other major campaign promises will need to wait, like the promised repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or alterations to B.C.’s no-fault car insurance rules. These will require legislation.

items.content_html:

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) suspended the official search for James “Dakota” Smith, a Ma’amtagila Nation member who went missing while canoeing near Sayward, British Columbia, on Nov. 6. His capsized canoe was found, but police said high winds, heavy rain and cold water had sharply reduced his chances of survival and made water and shoreline searches unsafe. Smith’s family and community continue searching and are seeking government support for a coordinated operation with trained teams and equipment. Storms across southwestern British Columbia prompted rainfall warnings, with up to 250 millimetres forecast in parts of Vancouver Island. Flood watches remained in effect across much of the island and the south coast.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Meta says it may withdraw WhatsApp if Canada weakens encryption
items.content_html:

Meta says it would consider withdrawing WhatsApp or other services from Canada if Bill C-22 passes without further changes to protect encryption. At a Senate committee hearing, the company argued the proposed lawful-access law could require providers to build surveillance capabilities or comply with confidential orders, putting encrypted data at risk. Meta’s director of privacy and public policy, Robyn Greene, said it was not technically possible to comply while continuing to offer secure end-to-end encryption. The Senate is reviewing the bill after Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree amended it to limit when companies could be required to decrypt information. The government says the legislation gives police and intelligence agencies tools to prevent and investigate modern crime, while Meta and other technology companies say the changes leave security gaps. Meta’s Rachel Curran said the company would review its options if the bill became law without further changes.

items.title: [Fast Company] All these outages show how corporate America needs to modernize out-of-date tech
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Over the past five days, a string of high-profile tech outages has left Americans struggling to send emails, catch flights, and access their bank accounts.

While the disruptions raised concerns about AI-powered cybersecurity threats, the real culprit may be something less sinister: corporate America’s tech systems are simply out of date. 

Outages like those at JPMorgan Chase, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and Microsoft can occur when computer systems are undergoing major upgrades, Marva Bailer, CEO of tech advisory firm Qualaix, told the New York Post. Bolting on new technology can leave the systems vulnerable.

Although it is unclear whether the recent outages were directly related to artificial intelligence, many organizations are currently upgrading their networks to handle AI tools. Microsoft attributed its outage to an issue that arose during a network capacity upgrade, according to the Financial Times.

The time of year could also be a factor, as technicians rush to make sure systems are ready for the holiday shopping and travel season.

“It’s holiday time, it’s travel time, it’s shopping,” Bailer told the New York Post. “So, you have all those higher spikes in volume and more pressure to [update your systems].”

AI is also allowing companies to identify software vulnerabilities far more quickly, possibly leaving IT workers with too much work on their hands, the Post reported.

Like Bailer, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to companies trying to upgrade aging systems, during an appearance on CNBC earlier today.

“[They’re] pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system,” he said.

The disruptions serve as a reminder of how cutting-edge technology is often still dependent on centralized, aging systems.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.content_html:

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Prince Harry and five others seek permission to appeal in Daily Mail privacy case
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, and five other public figures have applied for permission to appeal the dismissal of their privacy claims against Associated Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday. Their application, filed on Friday, Nov. 6, challenges both the High Court’s rejection of the claims and a later order on the publisher’s legal costs. The claimants alleged that journalists or people working for the publisher used unlawful information-gathering methods, including voicemail interception and deception; Associated Newspapers denied the allegations. After an 11-week trial, High Court judge Matthew Nicklin ruled on July 7 that none of the seven claimants had proved unlawful information gathering. He accepted journalists’ explanations that the articles came from lawful sources and said suspicion alone could not establish the claims. The claimants say the rulings are “legally and factually flawed”. In August, Nicklin ordered an initial payment of £9,544,355 toward the publisher’s costs, with the final amount to be determined at a separate hearing. He ordered costs to be assessed on an indemnity basis, which can allow greater recovery. Associated Newspapers estimated its defence costs at about £34.5 million by July 9. The Court of Appeal must first decide whether to grant permission to appeal.

items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

items.title: [orf.at] Drone strikes kill two power-plant workers near Ukraine’s occupied nuclear site
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Drone strikes killed an employee of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and a worker at a nearby thermal power station on Monday, Nov. 9, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said. The agency did not say who carried out the attacks. Moscow-appointed plant management blamed Ukrainian forces for the nuclear-plant worker’s death, while Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly accused each other of attacks around the site. The nuclear plant’s six reactors have been shut down since 2022, but safety systems still require electricity. On Nov. 8, the plant lost its sole 330-kilovolt external power line for about 10 hours and used emergency diesel generators for cooling and other safety functions until power returned. The IAEA has maintained a presence at the facility since September 2022. The latest deaths followed the reported killing of another plant employee in a drone attack on Oct. 29. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemned the attacks and called for them to stop. The agency has not publicly assigned responsibility for the strikes.
